crucian: The goldfish was bred in China from a close relative of the crucian carp.
When pike are around, crucian carp grow taller, deeper bodies that are harder to swallow.
ayu: Most ayu live for only about one year.
In traditional ukai fishing on rivers like the Nagara in Gifu, trained cormorants catch ayu at night.
tilapia: Tilapia was farmed in ancient Egypt, and pictures of it appear in tombs thousands of years old.
Many tilapia can live in both fresh water and slightly salty water.
bass: Its upper jaw stretches past the back of its eye, which is how the largemouth got its name.
It gulps down big prey such as frogs, crayfish and even small birds.
guppy: Male guppies are far more colourful than the females.
Guppies have been released in many countries to eat mosquito larvae.
mudskipper: Mudskippers dig burrows in the mud and carry gulps of air down to keep their eggs breathing.
Its eyes sit on top of its head, and it can pull them down into wet pockets to keep them moist.
trout: The pinkish stripe along its side gives the rainbow trout its name.
Rainbow trout first come from rivers that flow into the Pacific, in North America and eastern Russia.
catfish: The whiskers around its mouth are called barbels and help it find food in muddy water.
In Japanese legend, a giant catfish called Namazu causes earthquakes when it thrashes about.
piranha: Many piranhas are more timid than their reputation, and some kinds eat seeds and fruit.
Its razor teeth interlock like a zip, and it replaces them in whole batches.
barramundi: Its name comes from an Aboriginal Australian language and is often said to mean 'large-scaled river fish'.
Barramundi live in rivers but travel to salty estuaries to spawn.
koi: Koi are colourful varieties of the common carp.
Koi were first bred for their colours in Niigata, Japan, in the early 1800s.
burbot: A burbot has a single whisker-like barbel on its chin.
A big female burbot can lay more than a million eggs in a season.
eel: Young eels are see-through when they reach the coast, so they are called glass eels.
Grilled eel, unagi kabayaki, is a classic summer dish in Japan.
pike: A pike can have hundreds of sharp teeth, even on the roof of its mouth.
Big pike are nicknamed 'freshwater sharks' because they hunt fish, frogs and even ducklings.
salmon: Breeding males grow large, dog-like teeth, so chum salmon are also called dog salmon.
Much of the ikura (salmon roe) eaten in Japan comes from chum salmon.
arapaima: Its scales are so tough that piranhas struggle to bite through them.
Arapaima can grow to around 3 metres long.
sturgeon: Instead of normal scales, sturgeons have rows of bony plates called scutes.
Some sturgeons can live for more than 100 years.
electriceel: Most of its long body is electric organ; its vital organs are packed in just behind its head.
It gulps air at the surface and gets most of its oxygen that way.
aji: Horse mackerel swim in big schools and are one of the most eaten fish in Japan.
In Japanese, 'aji' sounds the same as the word for taste.
clown: A slimy mucus coat protects it from the stinging tentacles of its sea anemone home.
Clownfish make popping and clicking sounds to talk to each other.
sardine: Sardines are a favourite food of whales, dolphins, seabirds and tuna.
In South Africa's 'sardine run', billions of sardines travel up the coast each winter.
starfish: A starfish has a simple eye at the tip of each arm that senses light.
It eats clams by pushing its stomach out of its body and into the shell.
flyingfish: Flying fish beat their tails on the surface to take off at high speed.
Its roe, called tobiko, is the crunchy orange topping on some sushi.
bluetang: Young blue tangs are bright yellow and turn blue as they grow up.
Blue tangs often graze on algae together in groups.
boxfish: When stressed, some boxfish release a toxin into the water around them.
Car designers once studied the boxfish's shape to build a concept car.
puffer: A pufferfish's teeth are fused into a beak that keeps growing and is worn down by crunching shells.
A male white-spotted pufferfish draws round patterns in the sand to attract a mate.
tai: Red sea bream can live for more than 20 years.
Its pink colour comes partly from pigments in the shrimp and crabs it eats.
halibut: Halibut are among the biggest flatfish, and Atlantic halibut can weigh over 200 kg.
It lies flat on the seabed and can change colour to blend in.
seahorse: Seahorses swim upright and are among the slowest fish in the sea.
They hold on to seagrass and coral with their curly tails.
yellowtail: Farmed young yellowtail are called hamachi, a sushi favourite.
Yellowtail are fast swimmers that travel along Japan's coasts with the seasons.
lionfish: Lionfish use their big fins to herd small fish into corners before swallowing them.
Lionfish come from the Indo-Pacific but have spread across the Caribbean, where they are invasive.
moray: Morays open and close their mouths all the time to pump water over their gills; it isn't a threat.
Some morays team up with groupers to hunt together.
tuna: Bluefin tuna can dive deeper than 1,000 metres.
Its fins fold into grooves along its body to keep it streamlined.
sunfish: Instead of a normal tail, it has a rounded flap called a clavus.
swordfish: It slashes at prey with its long, flat bill rather than spearing it.
Adult swordfish have no scales and no teeth.
manta: A manta ray can measure more than 7 metres from wingtip to wingtip.
Mantas sometimes leap high out of the water, and nobody is sure why.
whaleshark: Every whale shark has its own pattern of spots, like a fingerprint.
It can grow to around 12 metres long or more, longer than a bus.
lantern: Lanternfish swim up towards the surface at night to feed and sink back down by day.
Each species has its own pattern of lights, which may help them recognise each other.
hatchet: Its body is very thin and silvery, shaped like the blade of a hatchet.
Its big eyes point upwards to spot the shadows of prey above.
grenadier: Grenadiers have big heads and large eyes for life in the dark.
Many grenadiers make drumming sounds with muscles on their swim bladder.
snailfish: Deep-sea snailfish have soft, jelly-like bodies that cope with the crushing pressure.
Some deep-sea snailfish are so see-through you can glimpse their insides.
bristlemouth: It is named after its rows of tiny, bristle-like teeth.
Most bristlemouths are only a few centimetres long.
angler: In some anglerfish species, the tiny male fuses onto the female for life.
Its stretchy stomach lets it swallow prey as big as itself.
blob: Its jelly-like flesh is lighter than water, so it floats just above the seafloor without much effort.
In 2013 the blobfish was voted the world's ugliest animal.
clione: It hunts another kind of sea snail and pulls it out of its shell with its tentacles.
In Japan it is called kurione and is a famous sight under Hokkaido's winter drift ice.
gulper: Its stomach can stretch to hold a surprisingly big meal.
The tip of its long, whip-like tail can glow.
viperfish: It has a glowing lure on a long spine of its back fin.
It swims up into shallower water at night to hunt.
dragonfish: Many dragonfish have a glowing barbel dangling from the chin.
Its teeth are see-through, which makes them hard to spot in the dark.
fangtooth: Its two biggest fangs slot into sockets on either side of its brain so it can close its mouth.
Fangtooths can live as deep as about 5,000 metres.
tripod: Its eyes are tiny, so it feels for food drifting past with its long front fins.
Each tripod fish is both male and female.
oarfish: Oarfish can grow longer than 8 metres.
Rare sightings of oarfish near the surface may have inspired sea-serpent legends.
coela: Its fleshy, lobed fins move in a pattern a bit like the legs of a walking animal.
Coelacanths give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
barreleye: The two 'eyes' on the front of its face are actually its nostrils.
Scientists think it may steal food from jelly-like animals with stinging tentacles.
goblinshark: Its pink colour comes from blood vessels showing through its skin.
Its long, flat snout is packed with sensors that pick up the tiny electric signals of prey.
frilledshark: It has around 300 tiny teeth, each shaped like a trident.
A frilled shark mother may carry her babies for more than three years.
goldfish: Goldfish were bred in China more than 1,000 years ago from a wild carp.
Goldfish can see ultraviolet light, which human eyes can’t.
loach: It can gulp air at the surface and take in oxygen through its gut.
In Tokyo, loach are cooked in a traditional hot-pot dish called dojo nabe.
carp: Colourful koi were bred from the common carp.
Carp-shaped streamers called koinobori fly in Japan on Children’s Day.
yamame: The masu salmon that stay in rivers are called yamame; the ones that go to sea are called sakuramasu.
Yamame live in cold, clear mountain streams.
archer: It aims correctly even though light bends where air meets water.
In experiments, archerfish learned to recognise human faces.
gar: Its eggs are poisonous to people.
Its hard, diamond-shaped scales were once used as arrowheads.
idol: It is often mixed up with the similar-looking pennant bannerfish.
Moorish idols are famously hard to keep alive in aquariums.
gardeneel: They catch tiny plankton drifting past in the current.
When danger comes near, they all slide back down into their burrows.
parrot: It grinds up coral as it feeds, and much of the white sand on tropical beaches came out of parrotfish.
Some parrotfish sleep inside a bubble of mucus they make each night.
mahi: Its bright green and gold colours flash and change when it is excited.
It grows very fast and can be ready to breed within its first year.
barracuda: It hunts by sight and is drawn to shiny, flashing things.
Its lower jaw sticks out past the upper one, showing off rows of sharp teeth.
mandarin: Instead of scales, it is covered in a smelly, bad-tasting slime that keeps predators away.
Pairs rise up together at dusk to spawn.
greatwhite: Special pores on its snout sense the tiny electric signals of living prey.
It can keep its body warmer than the water around it, helping it chase fast prey.
hammerhead: Great hammerheads pin stingrays to the seafloor with their heads.
Scalloped hammerheads gather in huge schools of hundreds.
sailfish: It is one of the fastest fish in the sea.
It can flash stripes and change colour while hunting.
firefly: It has hundreds of tiny light organs all over its body.
Not a fish, but a small squid about the size of your thumb.
vampire: It eats ‘marine snow’: tiny bits of dead plankton drifting down from above.
When threatened, it pulls its webbed cloak up over its body like an inside-out umbrella.
swallower: Its stomach stretches like a balloon to hold such a huge meal.
It lives deep in the dark ocean, often more than 700 metres down.
megamouth: It swims with its huge mouth open, filtering out tiny shrimp and plankton.
Only a few hundred have ever been seen, making it one of the rarest sharks.
giantsquid: It was first filmed alive in its deep-sea home in 2012, near Japan’s Ogasawara Islands.
Sperm whales hunt giant squid, and their skin can carry scars from the squid’s suckers.
